blind.0.see: Qualgo has contacted you 2 or 3 times. This time you said yes. The interviewer will ask themselves: *what changed?* If the answer is "NAB didn't promote me" or "I want more money", you look like you're running away, not choosing.

Now I've shipped the straight-through work, led AI adoption in our chapter, and built a consumer wallet end to end outside work. I'm ready to lead design for one product people use every day, and trust is the thing I'm best at designing."* (Q3)
blind.1.title: The word "Lead" in your old CV may have hurt you
blind.1.see: The old CV says "Lead product designer (14+ years)… across banking and finance". A recruiter read it and may have passed it to the HM. If they remember "14 years in banking" and now you say "10 years in product design", they will ask.
blind.1.fix: Raise it yourself before they ask, in round R1: *"One correction from my older CV: it's ten years in product design after four years as a developer, and about four of those years in finance. The new CV says it precisely."* One correction you make first builds trust in every number after it.
blind.2.title: "Enterprise designer" is a label, and it sticks hard
blind.2.see: NAB, LSEG, Green Koncepts and Hearti Lab are all B2B. People who build consumer products have a bias: enterprise designers make dense forms with no feeling, and care little about onboarding, retention or delight.
blind.2.fix: (1) Open your portfolio with the **consumer project** (the stablecoin wallet), not with SLE. (2) Use consumer words: activation, retention, first-session experience, delight, habit. (3) In every enterprise story, talk about *people*, not *systems*: "a banker at 11 pm trying to submit before a deadline". (4) Mention Merchant onboarding: it is a customer (SME) experience, not only a staff one.
blind.3.title: Your portfolio may not pass the 30-second test
blind.3.see: An earlier review of your profile found the portfolio could not be opened. Senior hiring people open the portfolio *before* they read the CV. If the first image is a grey banking data table, you've already lost for a chat product.
blind.3.fix: Part 8. This is the top priority this week.
blind.4.title: You will talk too long about process
blind.4.see: People from enterprise work and people who teach have a habit of telling the whole process. Your own profile also notes a pull toward "completeness over compression". At a scale-up, a line like "We did research, then personas, then journey maps…" will make the HM look at the clock.
blind.4.fix: The SEND formula. **Decision first, process after.** Every portfolio story starts with *"The key decision was…"*.
blind.5.title: Beyond visual craft, motion is the gap nobody told you about
blind.5.see: Qualgo's old Senior Product Designer JD lists "Motion" as an area of skill. Chat is a category that lives on micro-interactions: typing indicator, send/receive, reactions, swipe-to-reply, haptics. Your profile has no proof of motion work.
blind.5.fix: In the "safe chat" concept (🟦), build a prototype with 2 or 3 micro-interactions that each have a clear purpose (for example: a suspicious message "fades" with a warning; an identity check animation). You already have Remotion for demo videos. Talk about motion by its *purpose* (feedback, continuity, state), not only by its looks (Q23).
blind.6.title: You understand chat as a user, not yet as a designer
blind.6.see: Engineers (Persona 4, 6) will ask about message states, sync, multiple devices, E2EE and search, large groups, and notifications. If you answer like a user ("I'd make it simple"), you lose points.
blind.6.fix: Part 9 (chat glossary) + Q21. Learn the 12 states and the 8 classic edge cases of chat.
blind.7.title: Salary: you may be pricing yourself like an Australian bank employee
blind.7.see: NAB pays well and steadily, with bonuses. A startup may pay a higher base salary but give fewer benefits. If you ask for "NAB salary + 30%" with no reason, the recruiter will mark you as "expensive".
blind.7.fix: Part 13: work out the **total package** (salary, bonus, insurance, leave, stability). Anchor on the *scope of the role* and *market data*, not on your current salary. You have bargaining power (they came looking for you 3 times). Use it once, gently.
blind.8.title: Freelance work can be a plus or a landmine
blind.8.see: You are freelancing for a foreign client. Qualgo is a cybersecurity company. They will ask: is there a conflict of interest? Will you keep doing it? Is there an NDA?
blind.8.fix: (1) Check the freelance contract: is there an NDA, and are you allowed to show the work in your portfolio? (2) Decide ahead of time: when you join Qualgo, will you stop or continue? The safest answer for a Lead role: *"I'd wrap it up before I start. A Lead role deserves my full attention."* (Q64) (3) For NAB: has the freelance work been declared under their policy? If not, declare it now. This also matters for references.
blind.9.title: References: what might your NAB manager say?
blind.9.see: Qualgo will call your references. If Jack Trinh (your manager) doesn't know you're interviewing, you can't use him. If a referee only says "Minh is very good at process", it feeds the enterprise bias.
blind.9.fix: Pick 2 or 3 referees who can speak about **craft and leadership**: a PM or PO (Aaron Orellana?), a designer colleague you coached (Jenny? Trang Bui?), someone from Tech Academy. blind.10.title: Data risk: don't bring NAB into the room
blind.10.see: Qualgo is a security company. If your portfolio has NAB screens that haven't been cleaned (customer names, internal numbers, system names), the interviewer won't say anything, but will write down: *"shares confidential employer data"*. At a security company, this mistake is fatal.

whiteboard.strangers.model:
**Sample brief.** *"Users are receiving scam messages from strangers. Design an experience that protects them without blocking legitimate contacts."*

**C · Assumptions.** 1-to-1 chat (not groups). Phone numbers are verified under Decree 147. A scam detection model runs on the device, and it isn't perfectly accurate. Goal for the quarter: cut scam losses without lowering the acceptance rate of real messages by more than 10%.

**U · Users and risks.**

| Persona | Situation | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| Cô Hoa, 58, Cần Thơ, mid-range Android | Gets the message "It's your child, I changed my number, send 5 million now, it's urgent" | Someone pretending to be family |
| Anh Tùng, 31, sells online | Gets 30 messages a day from strangers | Blocking a real customer by mistake = lost money |
| Linh, 22, student | Gets an "easy job, high pay" message with a link | Job scam, OTP theft |

**P · Principles.** (1) A waiting room, not a living room. (2) Warnings are a budget. (3) The right action must be the easiest action.

**S · Flow and screens.**

1. **"Message requests" inbox**: kept apart from the chat list, no push (except for people with mutual contacts), no read receipts sent.
2. **Context card** at the top of the conversation: *"Not in your contacts · Account created 3 days ago · No groups in common."* This is information, not a judgement.
3. **Three risk levels**:
   - Low: only the context card.
   - Medium (one signal, for example a link): the link doesn't work until the user accepts, with a light note.
   - High (signals together: a stranger + asks for money/OTP + claims to be family): a specific **blocking screen**: *"This message asks you to send money from an unsaved number and says it's a family member. Call your family member on their old number before you do anything."* Main button: **Call the saved number for "Con" (your child)**. Second button: Block and report. Small link: I know this person.
4. **Three actions** at the bottom: Accept · Delete · Block and report.
5. **For Anh Tùng**: a "Business account" mode lets him get messages from strangers directly, but still keeps the high-level warnings.
6. **Error/edge states**: the sender deletes the message; the sender has been reported by many people; the sender is a member of a 3,000-person group (weak context, show the member count).

**Why the main button is "Call the saved number".** Impersonation scams work because victims don't check *through another channel*. A button that takes the user to another channel (the saved number) is the strongest defence, stronger than any warning text. This is the detail that can make the grader remember your answer.

**F · Measurement.** Rate of high-level warnings → block/report; rate of ignored warnings → later scam reports (lagging); acceptance rate of message requests (guardrail for Anh Tùng); "blocked by mistake" complaints.

**"If I had more time".** An "Ask family" button (share a screenshot of the message with someone you trust); testing the warning wording with people over 55; working with banks to spot money transfer requests.
whiteboard.community.model:
**Sample brief.** *"Design tools for admins of large communities (5,000+ members) to keep them safe and healthy."*

**C.** A community has several groups and an announcements channel. Messages in large groups may not be E2EE, or may be E2EE with limits (assume: E2EE; moderation is based on behaviour and reports).

**U.** Volunteer admins (not staff), busy, using their phones. New members. Spammers/scammers joining in large numbers.

**P.** (1) Admins are the heroes, so the tools must be fast on mobile. (2) Preventing is better than cleaning up. (3) Fairness, with reasons given.

**S.**
1. **Entry gate**: questions to approve members, agreeing to the rules, a "new member" mode (no links in the first 24 hours).
2. **Moderation queue** as cards: swipe right to keep, swipe left to delete, press and hold to ban. Each card shows *why* it's there (reported 4 times; new account; has a short link).
3. **Automatic filters on the device** using keywords the admin picks, with a preview: "this filter would have caught 12 messages last week".
4. **Slow mode** and an **emergency lock** during a spam attack.
5. **Moderation log** for the admin team (openness inside the team), and a **notice to the member who was acted on**, with the reason and a way to appeal.
6. **Roles**: owner, admin, moderator; each with different permissions.

**F.** Median time to handle a report; share of new members removed within 24 hours (measures spam); number of admins who give up the role (burnout guardrail); share of appeals that succeed (fairness).

**Links to your background.** Maker-checker in RegShield (two people approve), alert triage in CYBERhythm, running a Toastmasters club (real people).
whiteboard.linking.model:
**Sample brief.** *"Design the flow for a user to use our messenger on their desktop, securely."*

**C.** E2EE across many devices. Linking is done by scanning a QR code with the phone. Risk: scammers trick victims into scanning a QR code (this attack has happened on many chat apps).

**U.** Office workers who want to type on a computer; victims tricked with "scan this code to get a gift".

**P.** (1) This is the moment attackers like most, so it should be the most careful screen. (2) Users must know *what they are allowing*. (3) Easy to see and easy to remove.

**S.**
1. The computer shows a QR code + instructions: *"Open the app on your phone → Settings → Linked devices."* (The QR code can only be scanned from inside this menu, not with the normal camera.)
2. After scanning, the phone shows a **confirmation screen**: *"Link Windows · Chrome · Ho Chi Minh City · just now? This device will be able to read and send messages for you."* Buttons: **Link** / Not me.
3. **A question to stop scams** (only when something looks unusual, for example a location far away): *"Did someone tell you to scan this code?"* If yes → explain the scam and stop.
4. **History sync**: choose "Move my last 3 months of history" or "Start fresh", and explain why history doesn't come over by itself (E2EE).
5. **A notice** on all older devices: *"A new computer was just linked. Not you? Remove it now."*
6. **Device list** with the last active time, and removal with one tap.

**F.** Rate of completed links; number of devices removed within 24 hours of linking (a sign of a scam); rate of "Not me".

**Links to your background.** Authentication research on about 18 apps for the stablecoin wallet; the "security at the moment of value" rule.

| Step | 45-minute whiteboard | 3-hour test | What you say (EN) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **C · Clarify** | 5 min | 15 min | *"Before I start: who's the user, what's the goal this quarter, what constraints should I assume?"* If nobody can answer (a take-home test), **write your assumptions down**. |
| **U · Users & risks** | 7 min | 25 min | Two or three specific Vietnamese personas (for example: a 58-year-old mother in Cần Thơ with an old Android phone; a 30-year-old online shop owner; a student). A risk table: scammers, a controlling person they know, a borrowed phone. |
| **P · Principles** | 3 min | 10 min | Three principles for this task (for example: "Waiting room, not living room"; "Warnings are a budget"; "Every promise true"). |
| **S · Sketch** | 20 min | 90 min | Main flow first, then the main screens, then **error states and edge cases**. In the 3-hour test: 4 to 6 hi-fi screens for the main flow, and wireframes for the rest. |
| **F · Follow-up** | 10 min | 30 min | Success metrics + guardrails, how to test in the first week, and **what you'd do differently with more time**. |
| *(buffer)* | - | 10 min | Check everything again, name the files, export to PDF. |

**Memory trick for C-U-P-S-F: "Cô Út Pha Sữa Fin"** ("the youngest aunt makes phin milk coffee": Clarify, Users, Principles, Sketch, Follow-up). Picture the youngest aunt in the pantry (Room F) making phin coffee: she waits for every drop, no rush.
rubric:
| Criterion | 2 / 5 (No hire) | 4 / 5 (Hire) | 5 / 5 (Strong hire) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Product thinking** | Talks about screens | Talks about user problems and metrics | Reframes the problem, picks trade-offs, can say *what not to build* |
| **Interaction & IA** | A "happy path" flow | Has error states and edge cases | Has a system: principles that can be reused across many features |
| **Visual craft** | Tidy, but generic | Refined, consistent | Has its own visual point of view that supports the brand and trust |
| **Leadership & critique** | "I design" | "I help the team design better" | "I set the standard, and people still use it when I'm not there" |
| **Collaboration** | Hands work over | Works together with PMs/engineers | Breaks deadlocks between teams with evidence |
| **Communication** | Long, in time order | Clear, with structure | The first sentence is already the answer; stops at the right time |
| **Domain fit (chat, trust)** | Hasn't thought about it | Understands the ideas | Has their own view on trust in chat |
